constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Legal-ethical decision analysis under NASP, IDEA, and FERPA
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Resolve an IEE Request, Protocol Release Demand, and Section 504 Dispute
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Apply IDEA 34 CFR 300.502, FERPA, NASP Principles for Professional Ethics, and Section 504 to navigate a parent IEE demand, a copyrighted test-protocol request, and an unauthorized third-party data-sharing directive.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: After an IDEA team found Liam (Grade 5, outside ADHD diagnosis) ineligible because he earns B-minus grades with informal reminders, his parents submit a written disagreement requesting a district-funded IEE and photocopies of copyrighted cognitive protocols. Meanwhile, the principal directs you to email raw behavior protocols to a private tutor hired by the family, and parents ask whether testing accommodations exist without an IEP.
taskParts: Detail the district's two lawful procedural options and timeliness obligations upon receiving a written parent request for a publicly funded IEE under 34 CFR 300.502.
Reconcile parent inspection rights under FERPA with NASP test-security and copyright ethics regarding raw cognitive protocols, and address the principal's email directive.
Explain why an external medical ADHD diagnosis does not guarantee IDEA eligibility yet warrants considering a Section 504 evaluation for substantial impairment and accommodations.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Separate four distinct issues in the prompt: written IEE disagreement, copyrighted protocol copying, principal's private-tutor email order, and ADHD accommodation access without an IEP.

planningFrame.label: Professional framework
planningFrame.guidance: Cite IDEA 34 CFR 300.502 (IEE without unnecessary delay), FERPA parent inspection and third-party consent rules, NASP ethical test security, and Section 504 eligibility.

planningFrame.label: Action plan
planningFrame.guidance: Notify special education leadership to either fund the IEE or file for due process, offer supervised protocol inspection with explanation, decline emailing the tutor without written consent, and initiate a 504 referral.

planningFrame.label: Follow-up & ethics
planningFrame.guidance: Document prior written notice (PWN), provide IEE agency criteria neutrally, respectfully explain FERPA/NASP limits to the principal, and ensure the team considers any future IEE results.

successCriteria: Accurately states that under 34 CFR 300.502 the district must, without unnecessary delay, either fund the IEE or file a due process complaint to defend its evaluation.
Distinguishes FERPA's right to inspect and review educational records from distributing copyrighted test protocols, offering supervised review or release to a qualified professional.
Refuses to email raw protocols to the private tutor without explicit written parental consent because a private tutor is not a school official with legitimate educational interest.
Explains that IDEA requires adverse educational impact needing specialized instruction, while Section 504 can provide testing accommodations if ADHD substantially limits a major life activity.
commonPitfalls: Telling parents they must prove the district's evaluation was flawed or give detailed reasons before the district will respond to an IEE request.
Obeying the principal's directive to email raw test protocols to a private tutor without written parental authorization under FERPA.
Photocopying and mailing copyrighted cognitive test items directly without checking copyright, state law, and NASP test-security safeguards.
Assuming that ineligibility under IDEA automatically disqualifies Liam from Section 504 accommodations or means the external ADHD diagnosis is irrelevant.
sampleOutline: IEE duty (34 CFR 300.502): District must promptly fund the IEE (providing criteria and evaluator list) or file for a due process hearing; it cannot impose extra conditions or unnecessary delay.

Test security & FERPA inspection: Honor parents' right to inspect and receive an explanation of test protocols in a supervised meeting (or transfer raw data to a qualified psychologist) without freely copying copyrighted items.
Third-party privacy: Politely decline the principal's request to email raw protocols to a private tutor unless parents sign a specific FERPA written release.
Section 504 pathway: Clarify IDEA vs. Section 504 criteria and refer Liam to the 504 team to evaluate whether ADHD substantially limits learning/concentrating and warrants formal accommodations.

quickReference.domainLabel: Professional Practices That Permeate Service Delivery
quickReference.title: RIOT/ICEL Assessment, Psychometrics & Consultation Models
quickReference.purpose: Anchors NASP RIOT/ICEL data integration, standard-score psychometrics, reliability cutoffs, ELL language timelines, and consultation stages.
checklist: Collect data across all RIOT methods (Review, Interview, Observe, Test) and examine ICEL domains (Instruction, Curriculum, Environment) before concluding a within-Learner deficit.
Check test reliability (at least 0.90 for individual high-stakes decisions), normative currency (Flynn effect), and linguistic/cultural validity before interpreting scores.
Select the consultation model (Behavioral, Conjoint Behavioral, Mental Health, or Instructional) that best matches whether the barrier is skill-based, ecological, or home-school aligned.
formulas: Score scales and reliability: Standard Scores (M=100, SD=15), T-scores (M=50, SD=10; BASC-3 Clinical scales: 60 to 69 At-Risk, 70+ Clinically Significant; Adaptive scales inverted: 31 to 40 At-Risk, <=30 Clinically Significant), Scaled Scores (M=10, SD=3); Salvia/Ysseldyke benchmarks require r at least 0.80 for screening and 0.90 for high-stakes eligibility.

RIOT/ICEL and SEM: combine Review, Interview, Observe, and Test across Instruction, Curriculum, Environment, and Learner; compute SEM as SD times square root of (1 minus r) to report 95% confidence bands (±1.96 SEM).

Behavioral Consultation (Bergan & Kratochwill) 4 stages: Problem Identification, Problem Analysis, Plan Implementation, and Plan Evaluation; Conjoint Behavioral Consultation (CBC) partners parents and teachers jointly across settings.

Cummins ELL proficiency benchmarks: BICS (conversational fluency) develops in roughly 1 to 3 years, whereas CALP (academic language) requires 5 to 7 or more years—never mistake fluent BICS for academic English readiness.
decisionRules: When a teacher requests immediate testing for a struggling student without prior instructional data → prioritize ICEL ecological review, classroom observation, and Problem Identification consultation before standardized testing.

When an English learner speaks comfortably with peers but scores low on verbal cognitive or reading tests → prioritize evaluating BICS-versus-CALP status, native-language proficiency, and dynamic/curriculum-based data before suspecting a disability.

When two cognitive subtests differ slightly or an IQ index falls near an eligibility cutoff → prioritize reporting 95% confidence intervals around the true score and integrating adaptive and classroom evidence rather than treating a point score as fixed.

When a student's behavioral difficulties span both home and classroom routines → prioritize Conjoint Behavioral Consultation (CBC) to align reinforcement and data collection across caregivers and teachers.
cautions: Never assume nonverbal intelligence tests are culture-free; they reduce verbal demand but still reflect formal schooling, speed norms, and cultural familiarity.
Do not use outdated test editions, because the Flynn Effect (~3 IQ points per decade) artificially inflates scores and can mask genuine intellectual disability eligibility.
Avoid jumping straight from an initial referral to an intervention during consultation; skipping Problem Identification and baseline analysis leads to mismatched plans.

quickReference.title: Academic Supports, FBA/BIP, MDR & Student Crisis Response
quickReference.purpose: Anchors instructional-hierarchy matching, CBM decision rules, FBA/FERB behavior plans, IDEA MDR timelines, and suicide-risk protocols.
checklist: Run a skill-versus-performance (can't-do vs won't-do) check and locate the student on the Instructional Hierarchy before choosing an academic intervention.
Identify the maintaining behavioral function through ABC observation before designing a BIP centered on a Functionally Equivalent Replacement Behavior (FERB).
Screen immediately for ideation, plan, intent, and lethal means during any self-harm disclosure, maintaining continuous supervision and breaking confidentiality to protect life.
formulas: Instructional Hierarchy (Haring & Eaton) and CBM: Acquisition (explicit modeling/feedback), Fluency (timed practice/repeated reading), Generalization, Adaptation; 4 consecutive CBM data points below the aimline trigger an intervention change.

FBA functions and differential reinforcement: Escape, Attention, Tangibles, or Automatic/Sensory; BIP pairs antecedent supports with a FERB and DRA/DRI/DRO while anticipating a temporary extinction burst.

IDEA Manifestation Determination Review (MDR, 34 CFR 300.530): convene within 10 school days of a removal exceeding 10 school days (or pattern); ask if conduct was directly related to disability OR failure to implement the IEP; 45-school-day IAES applies only to weapons, drugs, or serious bodily injury.

Suicide risk protocol (NASP/C-SSRS): direct inquiry on ideation, intent, plan, and means, uninterrupted adult supervision, immediate caregiver notification, documented safety plan, and referral—never use no-suicide contracts.
decisionRules: When a student's reading accuracy jumps dramatically during an incentive-based Can't-Do/Won't-Do probe → prioritize motivational/contingency management and engagement supports rather than reteaching foundational decoding.

When ABC data show disruptive outbursts consistently end independent math worksheets → prioritize escape-function BIP strategies (teaching a break-request FERB, task chunking, and pre-teaching) rather than time-out removal.

When a student discloses active suicidal intent with a specific plan → prioritize continuous supervision, immediate administrator and parent/guardian notification, crisis handoff, and safety planning over preserving routine counseling confidentiality.

When an MDR team determines a student's behavior was a manifestation of the disability → prioritize conducting or revising an FBA/BIP and returning the student to the agreed placement unless a 45-day IAES special circumstance applies.
cautions: Never use time-out or classroom removal for escape-maintained behavior, because removal negatively reinforces and strengthens the exact behavior you aim to reduce.
Do not rely on signed no-suicide contracts or leave a student at acute risk unattended while calling parents or outside crisis agencies.
Avoid declaring an academic or behavioral intervention ineffective before verifying treatment fidelity and checking whether dosage matched student need.

quickReference.title: MTSS/PBIS Tiers, PREPaRE Crisis Systems & Threat Triage
quickReference.purpose: Anchors MTSS tier health benchmarks, NASP PREPaRE crisis triage, behavioral threat assessment, and family-school systems alignment.
checklist: Check Tier 1 core health (at least 80% of students succeeding) and implementation fidelity before expanding Tier 2/3 caseloads or attributing failure to individual learners.
Triage post-crisis students by physical proximity, emotional proximity, crisis perceptions, and vulnerability factors under NASP PREPaRE before assigning intensive support.
Convene a multidisciplinary threat assessment team to separate transient from substantive threats rather than applying automatic zero-tolerance exclusion.
formulas: MTSS/SWPBIS tier benchmarks: Tier 1 universal supports ~80%+ of students (3x/year screening, 3 to 5 positively stated rules, 4:1 to 5:1 praise-to-correction ratio); Tier 2 targeted supports ~10 to 15% (such as CICO); Tier 3 intensive supports ~1 to 5%.

NASP PREPaRE sequence: Prevent/Prepare, Reaffirm physical health and safety, Evaluate psychological trauma risk, Provide tiered interventions and Respond to mental health needs, and Examine effectiveness.

Threat assessment triage (CSTAG): distinguish transient threats (expression of anger/frustration easily resolved without sustained intent) from serious or very serious substantive threats (ongoing intent/plan requiring protective action and target notification).

Family-school collaboration anchors: Bronfenbrenner ecological systems (microsystem through chronosystem) and Epstein's 6 partnership domains (parenting, communicating, volunteering, learning at home, decision making, community collaboration).
decisionRules: When universal fall screening shows 45% of third graders below reading benchmark → prioritize strengthening Tier 1 core instruction, curriculum alignment, and coaching before flooding Tier 2 intervention groups.

When a school experiences a student suicide death → prioritize targeted PREPaRE triage for close peers and vulnerable students, caregiver communication, and safe messaging while avoiding large assemblies or permanent memorials.

When a student makes a vague angry remark with no plan, history, or means → prioritize multidisciplinary threat-assessment inquiry to confirm a transient threat and connect supportive problem-solving rather than automatic expulsion.

When family engagement in Tier 1/2 planning is low across a linguistically diverse community → prioritize bidirectional outreach, translated communication, flexible meeting formats, and community cultural liaisons.
cautions: Never mandate forced critical-incident stress debriefing (CISD) for all students after a crisis, because pushing trauma recounting on low-risk youth can worsen distress and secondary trauma.
Do not hold schoolwide memorials or share graphic suicide methods during postvention, as these practices increase contagion risk among vulnerable adolescents.
Avoid treating MTSS as a rigid waiting period to delay an IDEA evaluation when a parent requests testing or a disability is clearly suspected.

quickReference.domainLabel: Foundations of School Psychological Service Delivery
quickReference.title: IDEA Law, NASP Ethics, Equity & Research Evaluation
quickReference.purpose: Anchors IDEA/504 legal timelines, landmark case law, FERPA/test-security rules, disproportionality metrics, and single-case research validity.
checklist: Verify written parental consent, Prior Written Notice (PWN), and IDEA statutory timelines before initiating, changing, or refusing any evaluation or placement.
Balance FERPA parent inspection rights with copyrighted test-protocol security and NASP ethical duties whenever records are requested.
Evaluate both statistical significance and practical effect size (plus treatment fidelity and equity risk ratios) when judging intervention or program outcomes.
formulas: IDEA timelines (34 CFR Part 300): initial evaluation within 60 days of parent consent (or state rule), IEP meeting within 30 days of eligibility, annual IEP review, triennial reevaluation every 3 years, and parent right to public-expense IEE (300.502) or due-process defense.

Landmark law and Section 504: Diana (native-language testing), Larry P. (nondiscriminatory IQ use), Endrew F. (ambitious progress appropriate to child's circumstances), Honig v. Doe (10-day/stay-put), Tarasoff (duty to protect), and Section 504 (equal access for substantial life-activity limitation).

FERPA and test security: parents inspect education records within 45 days (sole-possession notes stay exempt only if never shared); protect copyrighted test items through supervised inspection rather than copying protocols.

Research and equity metrics: single-case control requires 3 demonstrations of effect (ABAB or multiple baseline); Cohen's d benchmarks (0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large); Risk Ratio equals target-group identification risk divided by comparison-group risk (1.0 equals parity).
decisionRules: When a parent submits a written request for an IDEA evaluation while the student is still in Tier 2 MTSS → prioritize obtaining consent and initiating the evaluation (or issuing PWN explaining refusal) rather than using RTI to delay evaluation.

When a parent disagrees with a district psychoeducational evaluation and requests an IEE at public expense → prioritize either funding the IEE without unnecessary delay or filing for due process to defend the district's evaluation.
When a parent asks to view their child's completed test protocols → prioritize scheduling a supervised protocol inspection that honors FERPA access while safeguarding copyrighted test stimuli.
When a researcher cannot ethically withdraw an academic skill once taught → prioritize a multiple-baseline single-case design across participants or settings rather than an ABAB withdrawal design.
cautions: Never assume sole-possession clinical notes stay exempt from FERPA once shared with a colleague, placed in a cumulative folder, or entered into a shared electronic system.
Do not confuse a statistically significant p-value in a large sample with meaningful clinical impact; always inspect effect size and social validity.

Avoid equating NASP ethical guidance with state law when they conflict; resolve conflicts by clarifying the law, documenting consultation, and adhering to the stricter legal mandate while advocating ethically.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Over-relying on a single IQ or screening score instead of RIOT-ICEL triangulation
misconceptionFamilies.description: Test-takers frequently treat a single global IQ score, universal screener flag, or vague teacher label as sufficient for diagnosis or placement instead of triangulating multi-method RIOT evidence across ecological ICEL domains.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Operationalize the referral concern first, then gather convergent multi-source data across RIOT (Review, Interview, Observe, Test) and ICEL (Instruction, Curriculum, Environment, Learner), actively investigating discrepancies across settings before concluding.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Blaming the student or rushing to special education before verifying Tier 1–2 fidelity
misconceptionFamilies.description: Candidates often interpret stagnant student progress as intrinsic disability without checking Tier 1 core-instruction adequacy or Tier 2/3 treatment integrity—or conversely, wrongly use MTSS tiers to delay a parent-requested IDEA evaluation.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Verify core Tier 1 adequacy (≥80% classwide proficiency) and documented intervention fidelity (adherence, dosage, quality) before attributing non-response to learner deficits, while remembering IDEA prohibits using MTSS/RTI to delay or deny an initial evaluation.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Designing a BIP around behavior topography instead of hypothesized function
misconceptionFamilies.description: Test-takers commonly select consequences matched to how a behavior looks (such as hallway removal for shouting) rather than what maintains it (such as escaping hard academic tasks), accidentally reinforcing the very behavior they aim to reduce.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Identify the ABC pattern and maintaining function (escape/avoidance, attention, tangible access, or sensory reinforcement) first, then build a BIP around antecedent supports, a functionally equivalent replacement behavior (FERB), and extinction of the problem behavior.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Ignoring cultural-linguistic validity, psychometric reliability, and disproportionality
misconceptionFamilies.description: Candidates regularly accept English-normed scores for multilingual learners or students with sensory impairments without examining construct-irrelevant variance, confuse accommodations with modifications, or miss systemic disproportionality patterns.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Evaluate cultural loading, language proficiency (BICS vs CALP), sensory-access fairness, and norm representativeness before interpreting scores; separate accommodations (access without lowering standards) from modifications (changed construct), and disaggregate systemic equity data.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Misapplying NASP PREPaRE crisis triage, threat assessment, and safe postvention
misconceptionFamilies.description: Test-takers frequently pick universal psychological debriefing after trauma, endorse public suicide memorials that heighten contagion risk, recommend peer mediation for bullying, or confuse behavioral threat assessment with punitive zero-tolerance suspension.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Apply NASP PREPaRE psychological triage (matching intervention tier to exposure, vulnerability, and distress), follow safe suicide postvention guidelines (avoid glorification and large assemblies), use CSTAG-style behavioral threat assessment focused on safety and support, and avoid peer mediation when a bullying power imbalance exists.

misconceptionFamilies.label: Misjudging NASP ethics, confidentiality limits, informed consent, and IEE legal duties
misconceptionFamilies.description: Candidates often treat student confidentiality as absolute despite imminent harm or suspected abuse, skip informed parental consent for evaluations, mishandle parent Independent Educational Evaluation (IEE) requests, or conflate equality with equitable service access.
misconceptionFamilies.remediationMove: Verify legal and NASP ethical thresholds: break confidentiality when required for imminent safety or mandated abuse reporting, obtain informed written parental consent before evaluations, respond to IEE requests without unnecessary delay (either fund at public expense or file due process), and align service allocation with equity.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Over-relying on a single IQ or screening score instead of RIOT-ICEL triangulation
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Triangulate across RIOT methods and ICEL domains before concluding
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer diagnoses, classifies, or labels a learner from one test score, one screener flag, or one informant rating without checking ecological or multi-method convergence.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which RIOT methods (Review, Interview, Observe, Test) and ICEL factors (Instruction, Curriculum, Environment, Learner) are still missing—and why might two informants disagree?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Examine the assessment scenario and circle the single data point (IQ composite, screener cutoff, or teacher complaint) that lured you into premature diagnostic closure.
stages.requiredOutput: Name the omitted RIOT method(s) and non-learner ICEL variable(s) (Instruction, Curriculum, or Environment) left unexamined.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Map the problem-solving sequence: define the concern in observable, measurable terms → collect convergent RIOT data across ICEL domains → analyze error patterns and cross-setting discrepancies (such as home vs math class demands) rather than averaging away disagreements.
stages.requiredOutput: Draft a 4-cell RIOT plan and specify one testable ecological hypothesis explaining informant discrepancy.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Apply RIOT-ICEL to two referrals: (1) a fourth grader described as "unmotivated" who scores low on a universal reading screener, and (2) a middle schooler rated high on inattention by the science teacher but typical by parents and the ELA teacher.
stages.requiredOutput: Write an observable behavioral definition for Case 1 and list the exact classroom observation and curriculum-alignment checks needed for Case 2.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-solve the missed assessment item and transfer the triangulation rule to writing a psychoeducational report that integrates test scores with error analysis and classroom recommendations.
stages.requiredOutput: Select the multi-source answer and justify how convergent RIOT-ICEL evidence makes the recommendation defensible to families and educators.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Blaming the student or rushing to special education before verifying Tier 1–2 fidelity
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Check Tier 1 health and intervention fidelity—without delaying IDEA rights
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer escalates a student to special education after an unverified or inconsistently delivered intervention, or illegally tells a parent they must finish Tier 3 before an IDEA evaluation.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Was Tier 1 effective for at least 80% of peers, was Tier 2/3 delivered with documented fidelity and matched to the skill phase—and has a parent triggered IDEA evaluation timelines?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the MTSS vignette for two distinct red flags: low implementation fidelity (such as sessions delivered half the scheduled time or classwide failure) versus a formal parental evaluation request.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify whether your original mistake was blaming the learner for low fidelity or misusing MTSS to obstruct IDEA evaluation rights.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Anchor decision rules across MTSS tiers: strengthen Tier 1 first when fewer than 80% meet benchmarks; match intervention to the Instructional Hierarchy (modeling/explicit instruction for acquisition vs timed practice for fluency); verify treatment integrity before changing tiers; and initiate IDEA evaluation immediately without MTSS delay when a parent requests one or disability is suspected.
stages.requiredOutput: State the exact next step required when intervention fidelity is low (coach/restore integrity before re-evaluating student response) alongside the IDEA non-delay rule.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Decide the next action in two cases: (1) a Tier 2 reading group shows flat CBM slopes, but attendance and coaching logs show the intervention ran only twice per week instead of five, and (2) a parent submits a written request for a special education evaluation during Week 3 of Tier 2 math support.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify fidelity remediation and consultation for Case 1 and concurrent IDEA consent/evaluation initiation (while continuing Tier 2 support) for Case 2.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
stages.instruction: Re-answer the missed MTSS or consultation item and transfer the fidelity check to a district-wide PBIS rollout that succeeded in a pilot school but stalled after expansion.
stages.requiredOutput: Choose the system-valid action and explain how monitoring adherence, dosage, and skill match prevents false-positive referrals.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Designing a BIP around behavior topography instead of hypothesized function

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer applies a generic consequence (like hallway timeout for classroom disruption) that matches what the behavior looks like while accidentally feeding its maintaining function.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: What specific antecedent triggers the behavior, what consequence immediately maintains it (escape, attention, tangible, sensory), and what replacement behavior serves that exact same function?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Trace the ABC sequence in the vignette and check whether your originally chosen consequence would actually deliver the student preferred payoff (such as escaping hard work via office referral).
stages.requiredOutput: Name the maintaining function shown in the ABC data and explain how the distractor reinforces it.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Construct the four-part function-based BIP model: (1) setting-event/antecedent modification (such as instructional match, pre-correction, chunking), (2) explicitly taught Functionally Equivalent Replacement Behavior (FERB, such as requesting a brief break or help), (3) immediate reinforcement of the FERB, and (4) extinction/neutral redirection so the problem behavior no longer pays off.
stages.requiredOutput: Write one matched antecedent change, one FERB, and one consequence change tied directly to the hypothesized function.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Contrast two students who both throw pencils during math: Student A throws pencils only during independent multi-step word problems and is sent to the hallway; Student B throws pencils during whole-group lessons and laughs when peers gasp and the teacher lectures loudly.
stages.requiredOutput: Identify each student function (escape vs peer/adult attention) and design two completely different FERBs and consequence plans.

stages.label: Retry & transfer

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Is this low score measuring the target construct—or construct-irrelevant language load, sensory barriers, low test reliability, or systemic instructional inequity?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Inspect the student demographic, language, sensory, or psychometric details in the stem and flag the validity threat your original choice overlooked.

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Misapplying NASP PREPaRE crisis triage, threat assessment, and safe postvention
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Match PREPaRE crisis tiers, threat assessment, and contagion-safe postvention
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer provides uniform crisis debriefing to all students, holds a large schoolwide suicide memorial, uses peer mediation for bullying, or equates threat assessment with automatic expulsion.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Which crisis tier fits each student exposure and distress level under NASP PREPaRE, and does this response prevent suicide contagion and power-imbalance harm?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Scan the crisis, bullying, or threat-assessment stem and flag any unsafe or mismatched response (blanket debriefing, sensationalized memorial, peer mediation for bullying, or punitive zero-tolerance exclusion).
stages.requiredOutput: Name the specific crisis-safety or PREPaRE principle violated by the distractor.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: Organize the NASP PREPaRE response hierarchy: re-establish physical/psychological safety and normal routines first; conduct psychological triage (physical proximity, emotional proximity, threat perceptions, vulnerability, coping) to assign Tier 1 (reaffirming health/psychoeducation), Tier 2 (classroom/small-group crisis intervention), or Tier 3 (individual trauma-focused psychotherapy); follow contagion-safe suicide postvention (small-group factual notification, no permanent public memorials, monitor high-risk peers); and distinguish behavioral threat assessment (transient vs substantive threat + safety/support plan) from zero-tolerance discipline.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify the exact PREPaRE tier or threat-assessment action required by the scenario and state why peer mediation is contraindicated in bullying.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Triage two school events: (1) following a student death by suicide, student leaders ask for an all-school auditorium memorial with a slideshow, and (2) after a terrifying lockdown, most students recover quickly with routine while three eyewitnesses show persistent hypervigilance and nightmares.
stages.requiredOutput: Design a contagion-safe alternative for Event 1 (classroom factual scripts, quiet support rooms, living prevention focus) and tiered PREPaRE triage for Event 2 (Tier 1 routine for most, Tier 2/3 targeted support for the three eyewitnesses).

stages.label: Retry & transfer

misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.familyLabel: Misjudging NASP ethics, confidentiality limits, informed consent, and IEE legal duties
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.title: Apply NASP ethical boundaries, consent rules, and IDEA IEE timelines
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.recognitionCue: The chosen answer withholds safety/abuse disclosures to preserve rapport, tests without written parental consent, ignores or flatly refuses a parent IEE request, or equates equal hours with equitable access.
misconceptionRemediationPlaybooks.repairQuestion: Does this situation trigger a legal duty to breach confidentiality, require prior written informed consent, or obligate the district to fund an IEE or file due process without delay?

stages.label: Recognize
stages.instruction: Identify the exact legal or NASP ethical obligation embedded in the vignette (confidentiality limit, informed consent, IDEA IEE procedural safeguard, or equitable service access).
stages.requiredOutput: State the legal or ethical rule your initial answer violated or overlooked.

stages.label: Repair
stages.instruction: State the binding legal/ethical duties: (1) explain confidentiality limits upfront and breach only for imminent harm, suspected abuse/neglect (mandated reporting), or legal mandate—sharing the minimum necessary information; (2) obtain informed written parental consent before initial evaluation or reevaluation; (3) when a parent disagrees with a district evaluation and requests an IEE at public expense, the district must without unnecessary delay either fund the IEE or request a due process hearing to defend its evaluation; and (4) distinguish equity (need-based resources/access) from equality (identical allocation).
stages.requiredOutput: Write the exact two-option legal duty for an IEE request and the exact threshold for breaking confidentiality.

stages.label: Targeted practice
stages.instruction: Resolve two legal-ethical dilemmas: (1) parents disagree with a district SLD evaluation and request an IEE at public expense, and the administrator asks you to deny it by email because the district test was thorough; and (2) an effective parent-training workshop is scheduled only at 10:00 a.m. on weekdays, excluding hourly-wage families.
stages.requiredOutput: Specify the IDEA-compliant IEE response (fund or file due process without delay, never unilaterally refuse) for Dilemma 1 and the systemic equity redesign for Dilemma 2.

stages.label: Retry & transfer
